extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; philosophers and general educated readers interested in ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for judging moral worth, justice, duties, and permissibility of actions (e.g., lies, promises, treachery), derived from a philosophical treatment of compassion as the root of morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as the basis of moral value
rubrics_metrics.description: Only so far as an action springs from Compassion, has it moral value; and all conduct that proceeds from any other motive whatever has none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents Compassion as the 'real basis of all voluntary justice and all genuine loving-kindness' and treats it as the primary ethical phenomenon from which cardinal virtues are derived. Includes discussion that other motives (egoism, malice) do not confer moral worth. Transcendental/metaphysical explanations are possible but not necessary for the ethical claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fundamental springs of human conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only three fundamental springs of human conduct: (a) Egoism (desires the weal of the self), (b) Malice (desires the woe of others), (c) Compassion (desires the weal of others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every human act is referable to one or a mixture of these springs. Moral worth is held to arise only from Compassion; the others are morally worthless or morally indifferent. This taxonomy is used as a diagnostic rubric for identifying the motive-source of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain evokes direct sympathy; pleasure does not
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct sympathy with another is limited to his sufferings, and is not immediately awakened by his well-being: the latter per se leaves us indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains this by distinguishing 'positive' (pain, need) which works directly on consciousness from 'negative' (satisfaction, enjoyment) which is merely removal of pain. Use this to predict when compassion will be aroused and when it will not (e.g., misery draws sympathy more readily than prosperity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two degrees of Compassion — negative and positive
rubrics_metrics.description: The first (lower) degree of Compassion prevents me from bringing pain on another (negative); the higher degree incites me to active help (positive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction yields the natural separation between duties of justice (negative: do no harm) and duties of loving-kindness (positive: help others). Use the distinction to classify actions and obligations as either refraining-from-harm or actively-helping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leading ethical principle: Neminem laede; immo omnes, quantum potes, juva
rubrics_metrics.description: Do harm to no one; but rather help all people, as far as lies in your power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as the general rule by which to test conduct and the leading principle of Ethics. The formula contains two clauses mapping to the two classes of actions (negative and positive duties). Use it as a top-level evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is essentially negative; wrong is positive
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice or wrong always consists in working harm on another. Right is negative and denotes actions performable without injury to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because justice's requirements are negative they can be enforced by coercion (the state). 'Give to each one his own' is interpreted negatively ('take from none his own'). This serves as a criterion to distinguish moral right from mere positive duties and grounds for legal enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty defined as omission causing harm; duty arises from obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Duty necessarily means a debt which is owing — an action the omission of which causes another to suffer harm; duties depend on an obligation entered into (often via agreement), except parental duty which arises from having brought a child into the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrows 'duty' to cases where omission inflicts wrong, typically grounded in agreements/relations (prince/people, master/man, lawyer/client, physician/patient). It excludes gratitude from being a duty since its omission inflicts no injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of injustice and justice (quantity principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of injustice in conduct varies as the amount of evil one brings on another divided by the amount of advantage one gains; the amount of justice varies as the amount of advantage which injury done to another brings me divided by the amount of harm which he thereby suffers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distinguish degrees of wrong (e.g., starving man stealing a loaf vs. wealthy proprietor despoiling a poor man). The text notes this measure is relative rather than linear ('indirect and relative, like the ratio of sines and tangents'). Apply this for proportional moral assessment and censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double injustice (treachery) as an aggravated wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Double injustice occurs when one who undertakes a special obligation to protect another not only fails in that duty but turns and attacks the very person he promised to guard (treachery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: appointed watch who becomes assassin, guardian who robs his ward, judge who is corrupt. Treachery evokes the maximum public loathing and is morally worse than merely great simple injustice. Use presence of betrayed trust as an aggravating factor in moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lies unjustifiable when used as instruments of cunning, but permissible for self-defense or necessary protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Lies are unjustifiable insofar as they are instruments of cunning and moral compulsion; however, falsehoods may be used for self-defence (against violence or cunning) and to protect oneself from unwarrantable inquisitiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text allows falsehood strictly for self-preservation (e.g., deceiving robbers, protecting family secrets, avoiding danger from inquisitive questions). It cautions that the restriction must be rigid to prevent abuse. It also notes exceptional cases (doctors, 'magnanimous' lies, Christ's reported untruth) and that promises extorted by violence are not binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promises extorted by violence are not binding
rubrics_metrics.description: A promise which is extorted by violence is not binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from the idea that the binding force of a promise depends on its voluntary nature; if forced, it lacks moral force. Use this as a criterion when assessing the moral and binding character of agreements made under coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity may conflict with justice and should be limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity is the foe of justice, and often comes into harsh collision with it; therefore equity ought only to be admitted within certain limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text suggests caution in privileging equitable considerations where they undermine objective justice. This serves as an evaluative warning when balancing fairness-based adjustments against strict justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: State's role: coercive protection, not moral engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: The coercive apparatus (the state) exists to protect its subjects from each other and from external foes; it is not the institution for the spread of morality, education, and edifying instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a principle for delimiting legal enforcement: the state may coerce to secure negative justice but should not supplant individual freedom by forcing moral conformity (warning against inquisitions, autos-da-fé, religious wars).
